column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The article gives the age of selection both as about 10 and as eight to ten; the entry's eight to ten was not repeated.

Entry says Ghezo had the support of de Souza and court factions; the article spells de Sousa. Kept the article's spelling in the text; it may be worth aligning. The article notes that even the year of the coup is disputed in the sources; the entry's 1818 was not questioned in the text. The Glele succession is implied ('Ghezo and Glele').

The article is internally inconsistent: it dates the start of the march into Venezuela to 16 February, before the Battle of Cúcuta on 28 February, and gives the campaign's span as 14 May to 6 August 1813. Only the span was used. It also says Bolívar issued the Cartagena Manifesto at Cúcuta to ask for permission to enter Venezuela, which does not fit its own sequence; left out.
The article does not mention the 1867 opening of Barmouth Bridge or the boundary of Meirionnydd; both stay in the entry only.
The article dates the conquest to between 284 and 282 BC; the entry gives 283 BCE. Only 283 BCE (the siege of Arretium, in both) was used, and the span was left out.

The article says recent excavations found the site first inhabited in the middle of the second millennium BCE by Ochre Coloured Pottery people, before the Painted Grey Ware levels; the entry says occupation ran from the Painted Grey Ware period. The earlier phase was left out. The article gives the lowest of nine strata as before the 3rd century BCE and elsewhere occupation from before 600 BCE; neither date used. Tourist figures for 2017 left out.

The article says the Ahlamu were first mentioned in sources of Rim-Anum, king of Uruk, and in texts from Mari, before the 14th-century BCE Amarna letter; the entry says they are named in cuneiform sources from the 14th century BCE. The earlier mentions were left out of the text. The article also names Ashur-dan II as a victor over the Ahlamu (via Adad-nirari II); omitted for length.

The article's paragraph on the Kshatriya Mer is malformed wiki text and was not used. The article lists Lawrence as an agent of the Rajputana Agency, not as chief commissioner; the text says 'holders of the post and of the agency'.
The article does not mention the first Battle of Homs (December 1260) named in the entry; only Ain Jalut is told in the text.

The article says he founded Patiala 'at the age of 57' in 1763, which does not fit his birth in 1691; the age was left out. It cites Satnam Singh for his conquests beginning around 1730, while the entry says from the 1720s; no starting date given in the text.
The article dates his rule from 1528 and the first capital to 1529; the entry's 'around 1528' for the founding was not contradicted.
The article dates Ercole I d'Este's arbitration to 1599, plainly a slip; no year given in the text.
The article does not cover the ancient peoples, Roman Lusitania or al-Andalus named in the entry; the text does not touch them. Population rounded from 537,556.

The article says that as a follower of Harbi he strongly supported Harbi's independence-oriented platform, while the entry says he favoured continued ties with France (as head of the council, 1967-1976). The text says only that he began as one of Harbi's followers and does not characterise either stance. The article calls Harbi's 1960 death 'mysterious'; rendered as 'unexplained circumstances'.
The merged canton is spelt Waldstatten as in the article (usually Waldstätten).

The clan article gives Amago Masahisa as 1488-1513, while the Haruhisa article gives 1494-1518; Masahisa is not named in the text. The clan article dates Haruhisa's death to 1562 in one list and 1561 in another; not used here.

The entry says that at his height he claimed authority over eleven provinces; the article says the shogunate offered him lordship over eight domains in 1552. No number given in the text. The entry gives the Gassantoda siege as 1543, the article 1542-43; the text uses the article's span, which includes 1543.

The article calls Amangkurat II's realm the Sultanate of Mataram and notes that the Babad Tanah Jawi treats Kartasura as a successor sunanate; the text keeps Mataram. The Babad's claims of patricide and of magic used against his wives are attributed or left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, mostly a family list; it adds little to the entry

The question whether the tomb counts as Goguryeo and so Korean, or Chinese, is contested; attributed each view. The entry says 'probably Dong Shou' and dates it 357: consistent with the epitaph's 289-357 dates for Dong Shou.

The capture of Analamanga is dated 'around 1610 or 1625' in the article; the entry gives no year, so the text gives none. Two accounts conflict on whether Besakana was the first house built; the text says only 'remembered as his residence'.
The 1387 treaty with Venice is told by the article before his Navarrese alliance; left out.

The article dates the Second Cambodian-Siamese War to 1549 in its heading and to 1555 in its text; the text gives no year for it. The article's lead says Chan was ousted by Sdach Korn in 1512 and fled to Siam, while its body says Sokuntbot deported him to the border in 1509 (at 24, which does not fit a 1486 birth); the text gives neither year. Troop numbers in the article (up to 200,000) are left out as they come from a traditional narrative. The renaming of Siem Reap ('Siam defeated') is told as a Cambodian account.
The article is short; the sections lean on its account of the aftermath (1215-1217). It does not describe the campaigns of 1213-1214 beyond Bouvines.

The article gives her canonisation as 1650 in the lead and as the synod of 1649 in the body; the text gives no year. The entry says her cult was restored in 1909; the article has the imperial decree of 7 November 1908 and the memorial day fixed on 11 April 1909 with celebrations that year. The text names no year for the restoration. The entry says she became a nun 'in old age'; the article says after Mikhail's death. The text gives no timing for her first vows. The 2023 naming of a square in Tver left out (minor, recent).

The article says the grandson Francisco Rojas completed the manuscript in 1604, while the entry dates the chronicle to the late 16th century; the text gives no completion year. The article says the Kʼicheʼ rulers forced King Qʼuicab the Great to leave Chaiviar; garbled as written, so the text says only that the Kaqchikel left under pressure from the Kʼicheʼ rulers and names no king.

The article places the Zafiraminia's arrival in the 14th century (after Racoube) in one place and in the 16th century in another; the entry says they ruled from around 1500. The text gives no arrival date. The 2013 population estimate (360,000) left out as an 'as of' figure. The 'Society' section's claim that the ancestors came from the north 150-200 years ago conflicts with the earlier history; left out.

The article gives his death as 1633, 1635 or 1638; the entry has c. 1635. The text gives no death year. The article does not say in this excerpt what Shirley did for the Safavid army; the entry's mention of firearms is left to the entry. His claim to have carried forged letters to the Duke of Parma in 1586-1587 is uncorroborated; left out.

The article dates him c. 2300 BC or, alternatively, to the Isin-Larsa period c. 2000-1900 BC; the entry says the late third millennium BCE. The text gives no date. The article places Naram-Sin's reign c. 2254-2218 and Satuni's defeat c. 2250; dates left out with the dating question. Short article; two sections.
The Ripley claim is told as the article tells it (with its error of age noted); the article adds that the gunshot cause Ripley gave is unverified.
The entry says 'several ironworks and steelworks'; the article says three companies. Not contradictory; the text names the three.

The article says the guild commissioned Michelangelo's David; left out as unsourced and loosely worded there (the Opera del Duomo, under the guild, is usually named). The entry's Ciompi revolt and the English and Spanish wool are not in the article.
The article is thin on his policies in Fiji; the entry's account of them is not repeated.
The entry says the town was founded after the Cantabrian Wars; the article's c. 14 BC camp agrees. The article's 'iurudicus' is given as iuridicus.
The article says the United States was covertly involved in the 1979 coup; left out as a bare claim without detail.

The article gives two counts of rebel dead: 9 killed in combat and 42 executed later (Moncada), plus ten at Bayamo; and Castro's own figures of five killed and 56 executed. The text gives the itemised executions and says Castro's figures differ.
Length given as about 140 km in the entry and 143 km in the article; not repeated. 'As of 2006' claim about Sloth Hole as one of three oldest Clovis sites left out.

SKIPPED: The article has about 200 words of substance (builders, materials, completion in 1902, the 1926 minaret, restorations, dimensions and domes); a text of 260 words would need padding. Note for the editor: the article says construction began in 1889, the entry 1899.

SKIPPED: The article is a short physical geography (about 200 words of substance plus lists of towns) and says nothing of the landgraviate or the Fürstenberg history the entry is about; too little to add without padding.

The entry says the Banu Kanz intermarried with the Nubians; the article says the Rabi'ah intermarried with the Beja Hadariba (sons of Rabi'ah fathers and Hadariba mothers inherited by Beja matrilineal custom). The intermarriage is left out of the text; only the Rabi'ah-Hadariba alliance in mining is told. The article's lead says the Banu Kanz descended from the Banu Hanifa; its Origins section gives the Rabi'ah-Hadariba line. The text follows the Rabi'ah line, as the entry does. The article's last sentence is cut off ('inhabit the Upper Egypt reaches of'): the text says only that the Kunuz live in Upper Egypt.

The article's lead says the church was built in 1888, while its history says construction began in 1885 and that the year of completion is not recorded. The text gives only the start in 1885. Left out: the 2025 flooded wedding and its photographs, as slight for a history page.

The article says moderates 'came to the House and demanded' abdication 'two days later' after 6 December, i.e. 8 December, while its lead says members voted to dissolve on 12 December, the entry's month. No day of dissolution is given in the text.
The entry says Elmet survived until the early 7th century; the article gives no date, so none is repeated. Left out: the present parliamentary constituency and its MP, amenities and local media.
The entry says Augustus granted the region to Herod in the 20s BCE; the article says only that Herod acquired it in the 1st century BCE. No date for the grant is given in the text.

The article dates the battle 12 July 1691 old style, 22 July new style; the entry gives 12 July, which the text keeps. The article describes Aughrim as one of the bloodiest battles fought in Britain and Ireland, with the caveat that poorly recorded medieval battles may rival it; the entry's 'perhaps the bloodiest' is not repeated.
According to a later conjecture by Huan Tan, Chen Ping's envoy warned Modu's wife that a victorious Modu might take Han concubines; left out as conjecture.

The entry says Charles was forced to accept Nominoë's authority in Brittany; the article says only that a treaty was made in 846 whose content is unknown. The text gives the article's wording without contradicting the entry. The article calls Ballon 'relatively minor' compared with Jengland; the entry calls it a key step. The text gives the scholarly confusion and the dating of Breton unity to Ballon, without either judgement in its own voice.
Sun Tzu (Sun Wu) is hedged as in the entry ('traditionally') and the article.
The article's three accounts disagree on whether the crown prince was captured (Dreyer) or escaped (Langlois, Tsai); both versions are attributed in the text.
The article's material is short (about 300 words); two sections only, the aftermath folded into the course of events.

The article's lead says the South Africans held the wood until 19 July, while its narrative has the last of them march out on 20 July and the entry speaks of six days; the text gives the 20 July march-out only. The article gives the South African brigade's losses as 2,536 for 1-20 July; the entry says only about 750 of more than 3,000 came out unhurt. Both can stand; flag if the editor sees a clash.
The article says the border was finalised with Bosnia Eyalet but gives no year; the entry's 1859 is not repeated.

SKIPPED: The article is one paragraph of about 230 words, most of it already in the entry (the siege of Handan, Tian Ji and Sun Bin, the march on Daliang, the ambush, the proverb); too little for a longer text.
The article says Allied losses were around 1,400, then itemises 1,062 Australian casualties 'including 800 dead'; the figures are not all consistent, so only the total is given.

The article says Kim Yu-sin and Su Dingfang surrounded Gongju before King Uija surrendered; the entry says the capital Sabi fell. The place is left out of the text. The article spells the general Kyebaek; the text uses the entry's Gyebaek, which the article also uses for the television series.
The article's lead dates the battle to 25 July 1850, its body has fighting begin on 24 July; the entry's 24-25 July agrees with the body. Left out the lead's single date.
The article gives 18 August [O.S. 6 August] 1805; the entry says August 1805, so the day is left out. The entry names Petar Dobrnjac as a leader; the article does not mention him.
The article gives the force that marched on Saint Helier as 700 men in one place and the first division as 800 in another; no figure for it is given in the text.

The article dates Xiang Yu's crossing to the twelfth month of 208 BC (the Qin calendar's year began earlier than the Western one); the entry dates the battle to 207 BCE, so the month and year of the crossing are left out. The article's 400,000-strong Qin army and Xiang Yu's army growing to 400,000 seem confused and are left out.
The entry places the battle in Guzgan; the article writes Juzjan for the same region.
The article places Maling in Shen County, Henan; left out the modern location.
The article's claim that the fleeing northern Xiongnu became the ancestors of the Huns is left out as speculative.

The article says Paoli was not present, then has him at his headquarters at Rostino above the bridge during the rout; his whereabouts are left vague. The article dates the annexation to the following year (1770); the entry says the island was then integrated into France, so no year is given.
The article dates the Treaty of Rhandeia to 64 AD; the entry dates the settlement to 63. No year is given for the treaty in the text.
The article dates the battle to 17 or 18 February 1370; the entry says 17 February, so the day is not repeated.
The article places the battle in the autumn of 1223 and dates Ibn al-Athir's year 620 to 1223-1224; the entry gives 1223 only. Left the season out.
The article counts 21 dead on Semple's side, including Semple; the entry says about twenty, so no figure is given.

The article says Shamash-shuma-ukin joined Teumman's coalition at the Ulai and dates Teumman's Sealand campaign to about 675 BCE, before his reign (664-653 BCE); both points look doubtful and are left out. The entry says Ashurbanipal installed his own candidates on the Elamite throne; the article does not say so, and its Kandalanu was placed on the Babylonian throne.

The article calls Córdoba an emirate in 920; the entry names Abd al-Rahman III of Córdoba without a title, so the text says 'the emir'. The article gives the location as unknown, within Navarre by both cited accounts, which fits the entry's 'in Navarre'.
The article has Toledo resisting until October; the entry says into 1522. No month is given in the text.

SKIPPED: The article is about the police squad, not the song the entry is dated by, and has under 250 words beyond what the entry already says (Yamagata's permission, 100 men, the attack of 14 March 1877 with 25 dead and 54 wounded, the revival of kenjutsu). The entry's dates are those of the song (words 1882, song 1885, Army March-Past 1886); the article says nothing of the song.

The article dates Lambert Visconti's landing and fortification of the hilltop to 1215; the entry has Pisa building Castel di Castro above Cagliari in 1216. No year is given for the landing. The article says she succeeded in January or February 1214; the entry says 1214.
The article calls the Mither Tap fort Iron Age; the entry says probably of the Pictish period. The fort is not dated in the text.
The article calls the Treatise of Garcia of Toledo an 11th-century work, though Bernard's archiepiscopate ran into the 12th century; the century is left out.

The article dates the second marriage to 1298; the entry says the county of Rodez came to Bernard in 1302 through it. Both are kept as they are: the text gives only the marriage year. The article does not say which wife's funeral required the loan; the text leaves her unnamed. Mons-en-Alarcon is spelled as the article gives it; the article's 'policemen on foot' is rendered as 'men on foot'.
The article does not name his killers; nothing is said of them. Authorship of the Chilean proclamation is disputed in the article (Miguel de Zañartu); the text says so.
The entry dates his Lutheran success to 1532; the article gives the January 1532 creed and the treaty of 14 February 1533; both stated as the article has them, which agrees with the entry.
The article's lead says the poem was 'composed by Adi Shankara' but its own section says it is traditionally attributed to him; the text keeps the entry's hedge ('attributed', 'tradition').

The article's remark that they are the second largest ethnic group of the province is left out as a ranking. The entry says the sultanate accepted Islam in the early 17th century under Gowa's influence; the article says the same and it is not repeated.

The article says the family was outcast in 1922 when Rameshwar Das Birla remarried; left out for lack of context. The entry calls the family Marwari; the article explains the term as a convention for Rajasthani merchants; the text keeps both.

The article gives the legion as 'IX Triumphalis'; written as Legio IX to avoid an uncertain title. The Sabis was thought in the 19th century to be the Sambre; only the present identification is given.
The article's claim of a 'hereditary dictatorship of the Chamorro' is left out as loosely worded.

The entry says he was killed in a riot at Goslar; the article says he was mortally wounded in a skirmish on 6 April 1088 after seeking help at Goslar, and died next day at Ilsenburg. The text gives the date and his death at Ilsenburg without calling it riot or skirmish. The article spells the anti-king both Herman and Hermann of Salm.

The article gives his birth both as 12 November 1879 (lead) and as Deepavali day, 13 November 1879, and his birthplace both as Madras city and as Wandiwash, North Arcot; day and place left out. The article says Chithira Thirunal issued the declaration of independence of 18 June 1947 supported by Iyer; the entry says Iyer declared Travancore would be independent. The text does not restate who declared it. The Punnapra-Vayalar figures of the article (about 200 killed at Punnapra on 24 October, 150 at Vayalar on 27 October) are summed only in Menon's estimate, which is the one given.
The article dates Philip II's conquest to 341 BC; the entry says around 341 BCE. The text gives no year to avoid repeating the entry.

The entry speaks of the Iberian Cessetani and Roman Tarraco; the article does not, so nothing is added on antiquity. Rankings of the article (third most populous region, second metropolitan area, most important chemical complex in Spain, most visited theme park) left out or softened.

The entry calls him the second emperor of the Tây Sơn dynasty; the article calls him the third and last. The text gives no ordinal. The year of the coup against Bùi Đắc Tuyên is given only as 'the next year' after 1794; left undated.
The body is written as the article names it, 'Guam Economics Development'.
The article's opening sentence is garbled; the text uses only what is clear in it.

The article spells the privateer both Robert Searles and Robert Searle; the first is used. The article dates Cendoya's administration to 1671 and the first stones to 1672; only the start of work is given. The entry's sieges of 1702 and 1740 are not retold.

The article gives his reign both as 1255–1262 and as 1230–1262, and says both that he was killed in 1262 and that the Pandyan intervention lasted 1262–1264. The entry says he invaded again around 1260 and was defeated in the 1260s. The text gives no year for the second invasion or his death. The article also says he spent more than 30 years trying to conquer Sri Lanka, which its own dates do not support; left out. The article writes 'Phrae Boromadhatu'; kept as given.
The article gives the restoration as 21 years in its lead and as 28 years later; the length is left out.

The article gives the dates as 1–9 September but also says the conference concluded on Wednesday 7 September, with a ball on 8 September; no closing date is given. The article names the Canadian ship both SS Victoria and Queen Victoria; left unnamed.

The article says the Song conquest of the Northern Han in 979 ended the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period; given as the article states it. Lau Nap-Yin and Huang Kuan-Ch'ung argue the northern invasion may not have happened; left out for length.

SKIPPED: the article is about Chettiar as a title used by many trading, weaving, agricultural and land-owning castes of South India (mostly a list of subcastes); the Nattukottai banking community of the entry gets two short paragraphs and nothing on Burma or the rice delta: too thin for this subject

The article's lead says the Chigils are known from the 7th century; the entry says Muslim geographers recorded them from the 10th century. Not a contradiction (the 7th-century mention is in Chinese-related sources and Ashina Helu's uprising), so the uprising is kept but no 'first recorded' date is given. The identification with the Chuyue and the Book of Sui mention are disputed in the article itself; told as Zuev's view; Atwood's doubt (2010) cut for length, but the text says scholars disagree. Left out: the Shatuo and Later Tang digression, Zuev's speculative etymologies of Zhuxie, the list of rulers.

The article says he replaced four kings; the entry says he deposed two. Both hold (he deposed Myeongjong and Huijong; Sinjong abdicated through illness, Gangjong died): the text names the four successions without a count. The entry's 1258 end of the last Choe dictator is not in the article (it says the regime lasted 60 years); not repeated. Left out: the long title lists, the Khitan invasion campaigns of his sons, popular culture.
Birth year: the article gives 1330, the entry 1325. Neither is printed. The article does not give the year of the Battle of Jinpo (the entry's 1380); the text gives no year for it.
Short article (about 350 words); everything usable is used. The legend of 1169 is told as legend, as the article does.

The article says Clonard 'fell into decline during the twelfth century'; implied in the see's removal, not stated separately. The 1113 plundering (Connor, King of Munster) carried off the riches of Meath lodged in the abbey church; shortened to 'plundered'.

The entry gives the 13,400-12,700 years date, the dimensions, the 1929 find and the debate on use; not repeated. Left out: the Mahaffey and Fenn caches (no Clovis points in the first, uncertain provenance for the second) and the Haskett point.

Dates: the article says the congress was held from 21 to 31 January 1920 (and calls 21 January the proposed National Day); the entry says 28 to 31 January. No opening date is printed. Abdyl Ypi's killers are named in the article (Sul Merlika, Salih Gjuka) with differing accounts of who was behind it; left out. Left out: the list of the initiating commission and the Paris delegation's internal quarrels.

The article writes 'Holly Alliance' (a slip for the Holy Alliance) as a second target of the common policy; left out, as the name is misspelt in the source. Haiti (in the entry) is not mentioned in the article. The article says the United States was invited only under pressure on Bolívar; left out for length.

The O'Connor kings and the 12th-century high kingship in the entry are not in the article; not repeated. The Airgíalla and Uí Maine are counted among the Connachta by genealogists but may be of other descent; left out for length.
The article says the document was written in 1549 (first draft November 1548); consistent with the entry's 1549.

Reign dates: the article gives c. 894 to 923, the entry about 898 to 916 (and d. 916; the article's own family section has George II reigning from 916). No reign dates are printed. Wife: the article says the alliance with Smbat was sealed by Constantine's marriage to Smbat's daughter, but its family section says he married a daughter of Adarnase IV. The text says only 'sealed by a marriage'. The ally in Hereti was Kvirike I of Kakheti; the entry says Constantine campaigned against the Kakhetians, so the ally is not named.

Arung Palakka and Sultan Hasanuddin (in the entry) are not named in the article; not repeated. The entry says governor-general from 1681; the article names him on 29 October 1680 and gives his taking up office on 25 November 1681: consistent.
Founding year: the article gives 1556, the entry's dates 1555 (its description says the 1550s). No year is printed for the founding. Left out: the list of presidents (empty in the saved copy).

Short article; all its substance is used. The inscription is paraphrased from the Spanish translation the article prints. The entry gives 808; the inscription's era 846 is the date in the Spanish era, but the conversion is not in the article and is not printed.

The truce of the first phase is the Treaty of Vordingborg (1365 in the lead); not named, to keep within length. The article calls the war both a trade and territorial conflict; the entry's framing is kept.

The Lashkar and the move of the capital to Gwalior (in the entry) are not in the saved copy; not repeated. The article mentions 'His wife Baiza Bai' right after Ranoji Sindhia, so it is unclear whose wife is meant; left out. The article also says he played a part in the Third Anglo-Maratha War; its saved sections stop in 1818 without detail.
The article spells the clockmaker both Kintzing and Kinzing (Peter Kinzing); only Kintzing is used, once.
The article spells the river Mereb; the entry Mareb. Not a contradiction; the article's spelling is used. Population of about 25,000 left out (not needed).

The article says 'the first election in Uganda prior to Independence saw the Democratic Party as the largest party', which sits uneasily with the entry's statement that it lost the pre-independence election of 1962; the pre-independence elections are not described in the text. The article contradicts itself on the Uganda National Congress (led by Musazi or Obote); left out. Left out: the speculative remark that the party may never regain its popularity, the 'Factions' section (opinion about the present government) and the 'as of June 2013' seat count.
The article is short; the text keeps to what it gives beyond the entry. The entry's 'cautious leadership drew mainly on the urban elite' is not in the article but does not conflict with it.

The article gives conflicting dates for Jayavarman II (reign 790-835; consecration in 802; establishment around 800; formerly dated 802-850 'without historical basis'), so no date is given for him. The article says the god-king was 'often attributed to Shiva or Vishnu'; the entry says 'usually Shiva'. The text does not generalise.

The article dates his rule 1208 to 1216 and his death 'around 1215-16'; the entry has c. 1208-1215 and d. 1215. No year of death is given in the text. The article says Charles I of Anjou's claim came 'about 60 years later' in one place and 'around 70 years later' in another; the text gives only 1272.
The article says he died 'probably in 1569 or 1570' (lead: c. 1569); the entry has 1569. The text gives no year of death.

The article says in one place that he died 'in Christian camp on the River Andarax' (near Almería) and elsewhere 'in the camp at Algeciras'; the text follows the entry and the latter. The article calls Violant his 'previous wife' at his burial but names no second wife; left out.

The entry says the Rabi'a 'settled there before Islam'; the article (citing al-Baladhuri) says the tribes were settled there by Mu'awiya in the course of the 7th-century Muslim conquests. The text does not say when they settled. The entry says that under the Abbasids it was governed from Mosul; the article cites Michael Morony for Nisibis as the administrative centre from Sasanian to Abbasid times. Left out of the text; it says only that Mosul was the main city. Article is short (about 330 words); the text is near the lower limit.

The article dates the tombs to the 4th-7th? centuries and mentions a recent re-reading of Jedar A's dedication proposing a 4th-century date; the entry says 5th-7th century. The 4th-century proposal and the uncalibrated C14 figure (410 ± 50 CE) are left out; the calibrated range 410-615 is given. Christian Courtois's link to the Kingdom of Ouarsenis left out for length.

The article says he 'appears for the last time in 906 and may have died then, though it is only certain that he was dead by 914'; consistent with the entry's d. c. 906. The entry says he let Arab raiders settle on the Garigliano; the article says only that he called in Saracen mercenaries from Agropoli and later besieged the Saracen fortress on the Garigliano with the pope. Not contradictory, but the settlement itself is not described.

The entry says the tower house was built in 1474; the article says Hugh Roe O'Donnell I built the castle 'in the 1460s or early 1470s' and founded the friary in 1474. The text gives no building date. The entry says Red Hugh O'Donnell partly destroyed it in the 1590s; the article says the tower house was damaged by 'the departing O'Donnells' (in the context of 1607). The damage is left out of the text. The article gives the grant to Basil Brooke as 1611 in one place and 1616 in another; no year is given.
The article gives no date for the law; the entry's c. 650-600 BCE is not repeated or contradicted. Neapoli and Neapolis both appear in the article for the modern town.
The article dates his death to 1553 (lead c. 1553); the entry has c. 1485-1554. The text gives no year of death.

The article gives his dates as c. 465 - c. 550; the entry says only 6th century. Not repeated. The biographical details (birth, healing of Peibio) are hagiographic; attributed to the accounts of his life.

The article places Kuiqiu 'west of modern Minquan County in Shanxi'; the location is left out. Jin's attack on Guo is dated 658 BCE and the conquest of Guo and Yu to the winter of 655 BCE in the article; consistent with the entry.
The entry gives c. 952-1000; the article gives 952-1000. No birth year is given in the text.

The article spells the stupa Ruwanweliseya; the entry Ruwanwelisaya. The text refers to it only as his great stupa to avoid two spellings on one page. The article names the brother who draped the stupa as Tissa and the successor as Saddhatissa; both kept as given.
The article says he was a Groom of the Chamber for 17 years in the lead and Groom of the Bedchamber from 1747 to 1764 in the body; left out.
